note: Subjects taught this semester. Edit freely, then run python3 build.py. gcr_link = the Google Classroom invite link (Classroom > class > Settings > Invite link); gcr_code = the class code. Leave both empty to show 'Ask in class'. Week topics are a standard outline: rename any week to match your syllabus. Files for each week go in teaching/<slug>/weekNN/ (see teaching/README.txt). video_courses = slugs from courses.json whose videos appear on the subject's Videos tab. File names containing 'note' or 'handout' go to Notes; 'practice', 'question', 'assignment', 'quiz', 'tutorial', 'sheet', 'problem', 'exercise' go to Practice; everything else is Slides.

subjects.title: Python Programming
subjects.blurb: Python from zero to a small real project: three lectures every week, each with a video, slides and a practice set.
weeks: Why Python, how Python runs programs, and installing Python
Decisions and loops
Functions
Strings
Lists and tuples
Dictionaries and sets
Files and exceptions
Functional style and modules
Object-oriented programming I
Object-oriented programming II
Algorithms in Python
NumPy
Pandas and visualisation
Python for the web and automation
Project, testing and revision

plan.title: Why Python, how Python runs programs, and installing Python
lectures: Why Python? Reasons, uses and the speed trade-off
How Python runs programs: interpreter, byte code and the PVM
Installing Python and running your first program

plan.title: Decisions and loops
lectures: if, elif and else; comparison and logical operators
while loops and common loop patterns
for loops, range(), break and continue
practice: Read a number and print whether it is positive, negative or zero.
Check whether a year is a leap year.
Print the multiplication table of n using a for loop.
Find the sum of the digits of a number using a while loop.
Print the first 10 Fibonacci numbers.

plan.title: Functions
lectures: Defining and calling functions; return values
Parameters: positional, keyword and default arguments
Scope, recursion and docstrings
practice: Write is_prime(n) and use it to print all primes below 100.
Write a function that returns the largest of three numbers without using max().
Write recursive functions for factorial and for the nth Fibonacci number.
What happens when a function assigns to a global variable without the global keyword? Explain.
Write a function with a default argument and call it in three different ways.

plan.title: Strings
lectures: Indexing, slicing and immutability
String methods and f-string formatting
Text-processing problems
practice: Reverse a string using slicing.
Check whether a string is a palindrome, ignoring case and spaces.
Count the vowels in a sentence.
Replace every space in a string by a hyphen and then convert it to title case.
Given "name=Asif;age=21", extract the name and the age into two variables.

plan.title: Lists and tuples
lectures: Lists: creating, indexing, slicing and changing
List methods, nested lists and list comprehensions
Tuples, packing and unpacking
practice: Remove duplicates from a list while keeping the order.
Find the second largest element of a list without sorting it.
Use a list comprehension to build the squares of the even numbers up to 20.
Rotate a list left by k positions.
Swap the first and last items of a tuple (hint: tuples are immutable).

plan.title: Dictionaries and sets
lectures: Dictionaries: keys, values and iteration
Sets and set operations
Counting and grouping patterns
practice: Count how often each word occurs in a sentence.
Merge two dictionaries. What happens to repeated keys?
Find the common and the different elements of two lists using sets.
Group a list of names by their first letter.
Invert a dictionary (swap keys and values) when the values are unique.

plan.title: Files and exceptions
lectures: Reading and writing text files; the with statement
CSV files and simple data processing
Exceptions: try, except, finally and raise
practice: Count the lines, words and characters in a text file.
Write the squares of 1 to 10 to a file, one per line.
Read a CSV file of marks and print each student's average.
Make a division program that handles ZeroDivisionError and ValueError separately.
Write a function that raises ValueError for a negative age.

plan.title: Functional style and modules
lectures: lambda, map, filter and sorted with a key
Modules and packages: import, math, random, datetime
pip and virtual environments
practice: Sort a list of (name, marks) pairs by marks, highest first, using sorted() with a key.
Use filter() to keep the strings longer than 4 characters.
Generate 5 random integers between 1 and 100 and print them in sorted order.
Print today's date and the number of days left until 31 December.
Create a virtual environment, install one package, and list the commands you used.

plan.title: Object-oriented programming I
lectures: Classes and objects; __init__ and self
Instance and class attributes; methods
Encapsulation and properties
practice: Define a Student class with name and marks and a method grade().
Create a BankAccount class with deposit() and withdraw() where the balance can never go negative.
Add a class attribute that counts how many objects have been created.
Use @property to expose the area of a Circle computed from its radius.
Explain the difference between a class and an object with one example.

plan.title: Object-oriented programming II
lectures: Inheritance and method overriding
Polymorphism and special methods: __str__, __eq__, __add__
Dataclasses and a small object-oriented design
practice: Create Shape, Circle and Rectangle classes, each with its own area().
Implement a Vector class that supports + and printing.
What does super() do? Show a case where it is required.
Convert a plain class with __init__ into a dataclass.
Design the classes for a library: Book, Member and Library. List the methods you would write.

plan.title: Algorithms in Python
lectures: Linear search and binary search
Sorting: bubble, selection and insertion sort
Recursion and an introduction to complexity
practice: Implement binary search and test it on a sorted list.
Implement insertion sort and count the number of comparisons.
Write a recursive power(x, n) that uses O(log n) multiplications.
Solve the Tower of Hanoi for 3 discs and print the moves.
State the time complexity of each of your sorting functions and explain why.

plan.title: NumPy
lectures: Arrays, shapes and dtypes
Indexing, slicing and boolean masks
Vectorisation and broadcasting
practice: Create a 3 x 3 array of 1 to 9 and print its transpose and its row sums.
Replace all the negative numbers in an array by zero.
Normalise a vector to zero mean and unit variance.
Time a Python loop against NumPy for summing one million numbers.
Predict the shape of the result of adding a (3, 1) array to a (1, 4) array.

plan.title: Pandas and visualisation
lectures: Series and DataFrames; reading a CSV
Selecting, filtering, grouping and cleaning data
Plots with matplotlib
practice: Load a CSV and print its shape, its column names and the first 5 rows.
Find the mean marks per department using groupby.
Fill the missing values of a column with its median.
Draw a bar chart of the five highest values of a column.
Plot a histogram and describe what its shape tells you.

plan.title: Python for the web and automation
lectures: JSON and calling web APIs with requests
Working with files and folders: os and pathlib
Automating small tasks
practice: Fetch JSON from a public API and print three fields.
Rename all .txt files in a folder to add today's date as a prefix.
Combine a folder of CSV files into one file.
Print the 10 most common words of a text file.
Handle a failed network request gracefully with try and except.

plan.title: Project, testing and revision
lectures: Planning and structuring a small project
Testing with assert and unittest or pytest
Revision and a mock test
practice: Build a small command-line project (for example a marks manager) with at least three functions and file storage.
Write five test cases for one function using assert.
Refactor one earlier program to remove repeated code.
Write a README that explains how to run your project.
Attempt the mock test within 90 minutes, then review every mistake.

subjects.title: Computer Networks
subjects.blurb: How data travels from one computer to another: layered models, addressing and subnetting, routing, TCP and congestion control, and the applications on top. Solved with real packets and GATE-style questions.
weeks: Introduction: network types, topologies, protocol layering (OSI and TCP/IP)
Physical layer: transmission media, signals, switching
Data link layer I: framing, error detection (parity, checksum, CRC)
Data link layer II: flow control and sliding window (stop-and-wait, Go-Back-N, Selective Repeat)
Medium access: ALOHA, CSMA/CD, Ethernet
LANs: switches, VLANs, Wi-Fi (802.11)
Network layer I: IPv4 addressing, classful addressing, subnetting
Network layer II: CIDR, VLSM, supernetting, NAT
Routing: distance vector, link state (RIP, OSPF), BGP
IPv6, ICMP, ARP, DHCP
Transport layer I: UDP, TCP segment, connection management
Transport layer II: TCP flow control and congestion control
Application layer: DNS, HTTP, e-mail (SMTP, POP3, IMAP), FTP
Network security: cryptography basics, TLS, firewalls
Revision and GATE problem solving

subjects.title: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
subjects.blurb: How to design algorithms and prove how fast they are: divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming, graph algorithms and NP-completeness.
weeks: Introduction: algorithms, the analysis framework, asymptotic notations
Recurrences: substitution, recursion tree, master theorem
Divide & conquer I: binary search, merge sort, quick sort
Divide & conquer II: Strassen's matrix multiplication, selection (quickselect)
Heaps, heap sort and priority queues
Sorting lower bound; counting sort and radix sort
Greedy I: activity selection, fractional knapsack, Huffman coding
Greedy II: minimum spanning trees (Kruskal, Prim), union-find
Graph traversal: BFS, DFS, topological sort
Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford
Dynamic programming I: principles, matrix-chain multiplication, LCS
Dynamic programming II: 0/1 knapsack, Floyd-Warshall
Backtracking: N-queens, sum of subsets, graph colouring
Branch and bound: 0/1 knapsack, travelling salesperson
P, NP and NP-completeness; revision

subjects.title: Data Structures
subjects.blurb: How data is organised in memory and why it matters: arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, hashing, searching and sorting.
weeks: Introduction: abstract data types, complexity, arrays
Arrays II: 2-D arrays, sparse matrices, strings
Singly linked lists
Doubly and circular linked lists; polynomial addition
Stacks: array and list implementations; infix to postfix
Stack applications: expression evaluation, recursion
Queues: linear, circular, deque, priority queue
Trees: terminology, binary trees, traversals
Binary search trees
Balanced trees: AVL trees; introduction to B-trees
Heaps and heap sort
Graphs: representations, BFS, DFS
Searching and hashing: collision resolution
Sorting: bubble, insertion, selection, merge, quick
Revision and previous-year questions

subjects.title: Compiler Design
subjects.blurb: How source code becomes machine code: lexical analysis, parsing, syntax-directed translation, intermediate code, optimisation and code generation.
weeks: Introduction: phases of a compiler, bootstrapping
Lexical analysis: tokens, regular expressions
Finite automata: RE to NFA to DFA; Lex
Syntax analysis: context-free grammars, derivations, ambiguity
Top-down parsing: recursive descent, left recursion, left factoring
FIRST, FOLLOW and LL(1) parsing
Bottom-up parsing: shift-reduce, handles, operator precedence
LR(0) and SLR(1) parsing
CLR(1) and LALR(1) parsing; YACC
Syntax-directed translation: S- and L-attributed definitions
Intermediate code: three-address code, quadruples, triples
Type checking, symbol tables, run-time environments
Code optimisation: basic blocks, flow graphs, DAGs
Local and global optimisation; data-flow analysis
Code generation; revision
